developer_message: You help an English-learning magazine's Fiction team turn a real, rights-cleared source into a reusable "Story Seed": an abstraction that keeps only the elements needed to write a NEW short story, and explicitly discards everything else (names, era-specific detail, subplots). This is not a summary for readers -- it is an internal planning document. Do not quote long passages from the source; describe things in your own words.
user_message:
[Source brief -- written by the editor, in their own words, not quoted from
the original]
This is Vsevolod Garshin's 1887 short story "The Signal" (Russian: Сигнал), in an early-1900s English translation by Lizzie B. Gorin, sourced from a Project Gutenberg public-domain anthology of Russian short stories ("Told by the Colonists: The Best Russian Short Stories"). Semen Ivanov, a sickly ex-soldier, works as a railway trackman with his wife at a remote watch-house. His only neighbor, fellow trackman Vasili, grows increasingly bitter about unfair treatment by railway officials: low pay, petty punishments over small things like an unreported vegetable patch, and finally being struck in the face by an inspecting officer after a minor complaint. Vasili leaves to seek justice through official channels in the city and comes back changed, worn down, and desperate. Later, while out gathering wood, Semen discovers Vasili on the tracks prying a rail loose with a crowbar -- an act of sabotage and revenge -- just before a passenger train full of people, including children, is due. Unable to talk Vasili out of it, fix the rail with his bare hands, or reach his watch-house and back in time to fetch a warning flag, Semen improvises: he cuts his own arm with his knife and waves a handkerchief soaked in his blood as an emergency red danger signal to warn the oncoming train in time.

[Task -- produce a Story Seed]
1. original_summary: 3 to 5 sentences, in your own words, summarizing what actually
   happened/what the source is about.
2. seed_elements: up to 5 short bullet-style strings -- the elements worth keeping for
   a new story (character relationships, situation, turning point, emotional core).
   Keep this list tight; do not pad it to 5 if fewer capture it well.
3. discarded_elements: short strings -- proper names, era-specific details, or
   subplots that should NOT carry over into the new story.
4. conversion_plan: 2 to 4 sentences describing how to turn this into an English-
   learning short story: whether to modernize the setting, what setting to use,
   first-person or third-person, and roughly how long/what level.
